pages.name: Every cable is a capacitor
pages.text: Every conductor near the hull is a capacitor. The copper is one plate and the hull is the other, with the insulation between. So a feeder has small capacitors from each line to the hull all along its run. Windings and drive filters add more. An insulated supply has no tie to earth. Yet it is joined to the hull through all this capacitance.[^1]

pages.name: Its reactance
pages.task: Each line has 1 µF to the hull. What is that capacitance's reactance at 60 Hz?
pages.why: A capacitor's reactance is 1 ÷ (2π × f × C). Here that is 1 ÷ (2π × 60 × 0.000001) = 2,650 Ω. With 254 V across it, about 96 mA flows.

pages.name: Charging current
pages.text: Each line charges its capacitors one way, then the other, 60 times a second. That flow in the line is its charging current. With 1 µF a line on 440 V, each line passes 96 mA. The panel draws the three as arrows, 120° apart like their voltages. Laid head to tail, they close into a triangle. So they cancel in the hull. Each line's current comes back through the other two lines' capacitance. There is no tie to the star point.

pages.name: Adding the three
pages.task: With no fault, each line pushes 96 mA into the hull. What do the three add up to?
pages.why: Three equal arrows 120° apart close into a triangle, so they add to zero. It works like a balanced load's neutral. A real system is a little unbalanced, so a little is left over.

pages.name: The way back
pages.task: With L1 faulted solidly, what carries the fault current back round to the supply?
pages.answer: The capacitance of L2 and L3 to the hull
pages.why: The current leaves the supply on L2 and L3 and crosses their capacitance into the hull. It runs along the hull to the fault and back through it into L1.[^2] The windings close the loop.

pages.name: Ten drives
pages.task: A 440 V system has 1 µF a line, and a first fault passes 287 mA. Ten drives are added, each with 0.1 µF a line in its filter. What does a first fault pass now?
pages.why: Capacitors in parallel add, so ten filters add 1 µF a line. C doubles to 2 µF, so the fault current doubles to about 575 mA. The larger the system, the lower its impedance to earth.[^3]

pages.name: Small or big
pages.task: You stand on the hull and touch L1, first on a small insulated system, then on a big one. Both are 440 V and healthy. Which passes more current through you?
pages.answer: The big one, as its capacitance to the hull is larger
pages.why: The cables' capacitance closes the loop through you, as it would for a fault. A big system has more of it, so less reactance in the loop. With 0.5 km of cable about 36 mA flows. With 4 km it is about 190 mA.
